General Language Notes: Always declare and initialize all your variables at the beginning of your scope.

General DB Notes: A database system is self-describing because it not only contains the database itself, but also the meta-data which defines and describes the data and relationships between tables in the database.
Insulation between the programs and data is also called program-data independence.
A view is a subset of the database, which is defined and dedicated for particular users of the system.
Instead of using joins, NoSQL databases often use techniques such as embedding and referencing to combine data from multiple documents or collections.
The simplest form of a NoSQL database is called a Key-Value database and it's designed kind of like a dictionary.

A Document database is a type of NoSQL database that can store multiple key values in a structure called a document. Documents roughly parallel rows in a table. Keys are scalars. And values may be complex data structures such as arrays or lists.
A Wide Column database is a type of NoSQL database where the columns are not fixed and the data is denormalized. The values can be complex structures such as arrays or lists.
A Graph database is a type of NoSQL database that represents a network of connected entities. Entities are liked by edges. Entities and edges each have their own properties that can be queried.

MongoDB: A collection in MongoDB is the same as a table in a relational databases.
A document in MongoDB is the same as a row in a relational databases.
A single entry in a collection is called a document.
A filter query fetches documents from a collection.
Operators are used to perform different filters or operations on a collection or a document.
Aggregation pipelines are used to perform aggregations or join operations on multiple collections.
Projection is used to select specific fields from a collection, reduce array data, and select specific fields from embedded documents.
GridFS is used to store large files.
PostgreSQL: PostgreSQL is an advanced, enterprise-class open-source object-relational database supporting full ACID compliance.
Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC) enables non-blocking reads and concurrent writes with snapshot isolation.
PostgreSQL offers first-class support for semi-structured JSONB documents with GIN (Generalized Inverted Index) indexing.
Advanced capabilities include Common Table Expressions (WITH queries), Window Functions, and pgvector extension for AI embeddings.
Redis: Redis is an ultra-fast in-memory key-value data structure store used as a primary database, cache, message broker, and streaming engine.
Rich native data structures include Strings, Hashes, Lists, Sets, Sorted Sets (ZSETs), Bitmaps, and HyperLogLogs.
Persistence is provided via point-in-time RDB snapshots and append-only file (AOF) operation logging.
In-memory execution allows sub-millisecond read and write latency across millions of operations per second.
SQLite: SQLite is a serverless, self-contained, zero-configuration, transactional SQL database engine compiled directly into the application process.
Transactions are fully ACID-compliant even across operating system crashes or power interruptions.
Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) mode enables concurrent readers while a single writer is committing changes.
SQLite powers mobile applications on iOS and Android and client-side web databases via WebAssembly.
DuckDB: DuckDB is an in-process columnar SQL OLAP database management system built for high-performance analytical queries.
It features a vectorized query execution engine and processes queries directly on Apache Parquet, Arrow, and CSV files without data duplication.
Like SQLite for OLTP, DuckDB is serverless and embeds with zero external dependencies.
ClickHouse: ClickHouse is a column-oriented distributed database designed for real-time analytical reporting at petabyte scale.
Data in ClickHouse is physically stored sorted by primary key in MergeTree family engines with LZ4 and ZSTD compression.
Vectorized query execution processes billions of rows per second per server node.
Neo4j: Neo4j is a native graph database implementing the Property Graph Model with nodes, directional edges/relationships, and key-value properties.
It uses the Cypher declarative graph query language to traverse complex relationships with index-free adjacency in constant O(1) time per hop.
Graph databases are optimal for social networks, fraud detection, recommendation engines, and knowledge graphs.
DynamoDB: Amazon DynamoDB is a fully managed, serverless, key-value NoSQL database engineered for single-digit millisecond latency at any scale.
Tables are partitioned across storage nodes using a Partition Key (hash key) and an optional Sort Key (range key).
Global Secondary Indexes (GSIs) and Local Secondary Indexes (LSIs) provide flexible query projections.
Vector Databases: Vector databases (Pinecone, Qdrant, Milvus, Chroma) index high-dimensional mathematical embeddings generated by machine learning models.
Semantic similarity between concepts is calculated using distance metrics: Cosine Similarity, Euclidean Distance (L2), and Dot Product.
Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) indexing structures such as HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) and IVFFlat provide sub-linear search speed.

System Architecture.introduction: Computer Architecture investigates hardware abstraction layers, CPU microarchitecture, and memory hierarchies that execute machine instructions.
System Architecture.remediation: Focus on latency numbers (CPU cache vs RAM vs Disk) and instruction pipelining hazards (data, structural, control).
System Architecture.deep_dive: Modern CPUs utilize Von Neumann architecture with separate caches (Harvard architecture in L1). Execution stages include Fetch, Decode, Execute, Memory Access, and Writeback. Out-of-order execution, speculative execution, branch prediction, and multi-level caching (L1 1ns, L2 4ns, L3 10ns, DRAM 100ns) mitigate the von Neumann memory wall.

True-False.statement: L1 cache access latency is typically faster than main memory (DRAM) access by more than an order of magnitude.
True-False.explanation: L1 cache takes ~1 nanosecond (a few CPU cycles), whereas DRAM takes ~100 nanoseconds (~200 CPU cycles).

True-False.statement: In a pure Von Neumann architecture, instructions and data are stored in completely separate physical memory address spaces.
True-False.explanation: In Von Neumann architecture, data and instructions share the same memory space. The Harvard architecture separates instruction and data memory.

True-False.statement: A Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) caches recent virtual-to-physical address translations to accelerate memory lookups.
True-False.explanation: The TLB is a hardware MMU cache specifically designed to avoid costly page table walks in RAM.

True-False.statement: Virtual memory translation uses the Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) as a hardware cache to avoid accessing page tables in main memory on every instruction.
True-False.explanation: The TLB caches recent virtual-to-physical address mappings, reducing average memory translation latency to near-L1 cache speeds.

True-False.statement: In a Little-Endian architecture, the most significant byte of a multi-byte word is stored at the lowest memory address.
True-False.explanation: Little-Endian stores the LEAST significant byte at the lowest address. Big-Endian stores the most significant byte first.

True-False.statement: Direct Memory Access (DMA) allows high-speed I/O devices to transfer data directly to and from main memory without continuous CPU intervention.
True-False.explanation: DMA controllers transfer blocks of data between I/O channels and memory independently, only interrupting the CPU when the transfer is complete.

True-False.statement: Branch predictors in modern superscalar CPUs speculatively execute instructions before conditional branch outcomes are definitively resolved.
True-False.explanation: If the prediction is correct, pipeline stalls are avoided. If incorrect, speculative results are flushed.

True-False.statement: A cache Write-Through policy updates main memory immediately on every write, whereas Write-Back only writes dirty blocks when evicted.
True-False.explanation: Write-Through ensures memory is always coherent with cache, but incurs high write traffic. Write-Back minimizes bus traffic by delaying writes.

True-False.statement: SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) execution performs different operations on identical data elements simultaneously.
True-False.explanation: SIMD executes the SAME operation across multiple data points in parallel using wide vector registers.

True-False.statement: Register Renaming eliminates false data dependencies such as Write-After-Read (WAR) and Write-After-Write (WAW) hazards.
True-False.explanation: By mapping architectural register names to a larger pool of physical registers, the processor allows independent instructions to execute out of order.

Artificial Intelligence.introduction: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning encompass computational models that learn representations, patterns, and decision functions from data.
Artificial Intelligence.remediation: Review linear transformations, non-linear activation functions, backpropagation gradients, and attention weighting mechanisms.
Artificial Intelligence.deep_dive: Deep learning builds layered parameterized representations: z = W*x + b, followed by non-linear activations (ReLU, GELU, Sigmoid). Training computes loss L(y_hat, y) and uses the chain rule (Backpropagation) to calculate dL/dW, updated via Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) or Adam. Transformers replace recurrence with Multi-Head Self-Attention: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(Q*K^T / sqrt(d_k)) * V.

True-False.statement: Without non-linear activation functions, a multi-layer neural network collapses into an equivalent single-layer linear model.
True-False.explanation: A composition of linear functions (W2 * W1 * x) is mathematically identical to a single linear function (W_combined * x).

True-False.statement: The Scaled Dot-Product Attention in Transformers divides by sqrt(d_k) to prevent dot products from growing excessively large and driving softmax into regions with vanishingly small gradients.
True-False.explanation: For large projection dimensions d_k, dot products grow large in magnitude, causing softmax gradients to vanish unless scaled by sqrt(d_k).

True-False.statement: Backpropagation computes the Hessian matrix of second-order derivatives to update weights.
True-False.explanation: Standard backpropagation computes first-order partial derivatives (gradient vector), not the expensive second-order Hessian matrix.

True-False.statement: Without non-linear activation functions (like ReLU or GELU), a deep neural network with 100 hidden layers has no more representational capacity than a single-layer linear regression model.
True-False.explanation: The composition of linear functions W_n * ... * W_1 * x is mathematically equivalent to a single linear transformation W_combined * x.

True-False.statement: Overfitting occurs when a machine learning model achieves high training accuracy but generalizes poorly to unseen validation or test data.
True-False.explanation: Overfitting means the model has memorized noise in the training set rather than learning true generalizable relationships.

True-False.statement: Dropout randomly zeroes out a fraction of neuron activations during evaluation/inference to ensure deterministic output.
True-False.explanation: Dropout is active ONLY during training to prevent co-adaptation. During evaluation/inference, all weights are active and scaled.

True-False.statement: In self-attention mechanisms, computation of the attention weight matrix scales quadratically O(N^2) with input sequence length N.
True-False.explanation: Every token attends to every other token, producing an N x N matrix multiplication (Query * Key^T).

True-False.statement: The Adam optimizer maintains running exponentially decaying averages of past gradients (first moment) and squared gradients (second moment).
True-False.explanation: Adam adapts per-parameter learning rates using both momentum (1st moment) and variance scaling (2nd moment).

True-False.statement: In K-Means clustering, the optimal number of clusters K is determined automatically by the algorithm without any hyperparameter specification.
True-False.explanation: K is a required input hyperparameter. Techniques like the Elbow Method or Silhouette Score are used to pick K.

True-False.statement: Residual connections (skip connections) mitigate vanishing gradients in very deep networks by providing an identity gradient highway during backpropagation.
True-False.explanation: Because d/dx (F(x) + x) = F'(x) + 1, gradients can flow back through the '+1' identity term without being exponentially degraded.

True-False.statement: The vanishing gradient problem in deep networks was significantly mitigated by replacing Sigmoid activations with Rectified Linear Units (ReLU).
True-False.explanation: ReLU has a constant derivative of 1.0 for positive inputs, preventing gradients from decaying to near-zero across many layers.

True-False.statement: In unsupervised learning, training datasets must contain ground-truth human labels for every sample.
True-False.explanation: Unsupervised learning (e.g. K-means, PCA, autoencoders) discovers hidden patterns without explicit ground-truth labels.

True-False.statement: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) trains a reward model to align LLM completions with human preferences.
True-False.explanation: RLHF uses Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) against a learned reward model to guide generative outputs.

Operating Systems.introduction: An Operating System manages hardware resources, provides abstraction interfaces, and schedules concurrent process and thread executions.
Operating Systems.remediation: Focus on memory management (pages, frames, page faults), process states, and synchronization primitives (mutex, semaphore, spinlock).
Operating Systems.deep_dive: The OS kernel operates in privileged ring 0. Processes possess isolated virtual address spaces mapped via page tables to physical frames; threads share memory within a parent process. Context switching saves register state and flushes/updates TLB. Deadlock occurs when four Coffman conditions hold simultaneously: Mutual Exclusion, Hold and Wait, No Preemption, and Circular Wait.

True-False.statement: Threads belonging to the same process share the same heap memory and open file descriptors, but each maintains its own call stack and program counter.
True-False.explanation: Threads share process resources (heap, data, file handles) for low-overhead concurrency, while retaining independent execution stacks and registers.

True-False.statement: A spinlock is more CPU-efficient than a mutex when the critical section is expected to take milliseconds to complete.
True-False.explanation: Spinlocks busy-wait (burning CPU cycles); for operations longer than context-switch overhead, blocking mutexes that put the thread to sleep are vastly more efficient.

True-False.statement: Breaking any single one of the four Coffman conditions prevents system deadlock from occurring.
True-False.explanation: All four conditions must hold simultaneously for a deadlock to exist; breaking any one guarantees deadlock freedom.

True-False.statement: Threads belonging to the same process share the process's heap memory, global variables, and open file descriptors.
True-False.explanation: Threads share virtual address space, heap, and open handles, while maintaining individual program counters, registers, and stacks.

True-False.statement: A page fault occurs only when physical RAM is physically damaged or has hardware memory bit rot.
True-False.explanation: A page fault is an ordinary CPU exception raised when a requested virtual page is not currently mapped in physical RAM (e.g., swapped to disk).

True-False.statement: In preemptive CPU scheduling, the operating system kernel can forcibly suspend a currently running process to run another process.
True-False.explanation: Preemption allows the scheduler to enforce fair time-slicing via hardware timer interrupts.

True-False.statement: Thrashing is a state in which the OS spends significantly more time swapping pages between disk and RAM than executing actual application code.
True-False.explanation: Thrashing occurs when the total working sets of active processes exceed available physical memory.

True-False.statement: Spinlocks are optimal for synchronization when waiting threads are expected to wait for long periods of time (multiple seconds).
True-False.explanation: Spinlocks busy-wait in a tight loop burning CPU cycles. They are only appropriate for extremely brief critical sections in multicore kernels.

True-False.statement: The Copy-on-Write (CoW) optimization defers duplicating memory pages after a fork() system call until either process writes to a page.
True-False.explanation: Both parent and child share read-only pages until a write triggers a page fault that duplicates only the modified page.

True-False.statement: All four Coffman conditions (Mutual Exclusion, Hold and Wait, No Preemption, Circular Wait) must simultaneously hold for deadlock to occur.
True-False.explanation: If any one of the four Coffman conditions is broken, deadlock cannot occur.

Computer Networking.introduction: Computer Networking provides packet transmission protocols, routing topologies, and reliable socket communications across distributed endpoints.
Computer Networking.remediation: Study the OSI 7 layers, TCP flow/congestion control, 3-way handshakes, and UDP versus TCP trade-offs.
Computer Networking.deep_dive: Data travels down the OSI stack by encapsulation: Application (HTTP/DNS) -> Transport (TCP/UDP segments) -> Network (IP packets) -> Data Link (Ethernet frames) -> Physical (bits). TCP provides reliable, ordered, error-checked streams using SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK 3-way handshake, sliding window flow control, and AIMD congestion control. UDP provides connectionless, lightweight, low-latency datagrams without retransmission guarantees.

True-False.statement: TCP uses a 3-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) to establish sequence numbers before transmitting payload data.
True-False.explanation: The 3-way handshake synchronizes sequence numbers (ISN) in both directions and confirms bidirectional reachability.

True-False.statement: HTTP/3 runs over TCP with TLS 1.3 encryption.
True-False.explanation: HTTP/3 runs over QUIC, which is built on top of UDP to eliminate Head-of-Line (HoL) blocking.

True-False.statement: TCP provides reliable, in-order byte stream delivery with congestion control, while UDP provides connectionless, best-effort datagram delivery.
True-False.explanation: TCP incorporates acknowledgments, retransmissions, and window-based congestion control; UDP delivers datagrams with minimal overhead.

True-False.statement: IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses providing ~4.3 billion unique IPs, whereas IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses providing 3.4 x 10^38 unique IPs.
True-False.explanation: IPv6 solved IPv4 address exhaustion by expanding address width from 32 to 128 bits.

True-False.statement: The Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) translates a domain name (e.g. google.com) directly to a MAC address.
True-False.explanation: DNS resolves domain names to IP addresses. ARP resolves an IPv4 address to a local physical Layer 2 MAC address.

True-False.statement: HTTPS encrypts the HTTP payload using Transport Layer Security (TLS) over TCP port 443.
True-False.explanation: HTTPS runs standard HTTP over an encrypted TLS connection, ensuring confidentiality and integrity.

True-False.statement: HTTP/1.1 allows head-of-line blocking on a single TCP connection, whereas HTTP/2 multiplexes streams concurrently over one connection.
True-False.explanation: HTTP/2 introduces binary framing and multiplexed virtual streams, preventing slow requests from stalling others on the same socket.

True-False.statement: A subnet with CIDR prefix /24 contains 256 total IP addresses, of which 254 are assignable to host network interfaces.
True-False.explanation: Network address (.0) and broadcast address (.255) are reserved, leaving 254 usable host addresses.

True-False.statement: Network Address Translation (NAT) maps private RFC 1918 IP addresses to one or more public IP addresses at the router boundary.
True-False.explanation: NAT / NAPT re-writes IP headers and port numbers to allow multiple private LAN devices to share public IPs.

Algorithms & Asymptotic Complexity.introduction: Algorithm analysis examines the computational resources (time and space) required to solve a problem as a function of input size N.
Algorithms & Asymptotic Complexity.remediation: Review Big-O upper bounds, logarithmic vs linear vs polynomial growth rates, and Divide-and-Conquer recurrence relations.
Algorithms & Asymptotic Complexity.deep_dive: Asymptotic analysis classifies algorithm scalability: Big-O (f(n) <= c*g(n)) gives asymptotic upper bound; Big-Omega gives lower bound; Big-Theta gives tight bound. Divide and conquer algorithms follow T(n) = a*T(n/b) + f(n), evaluated via the Master Theorem. Comparison-based sorting algorithms have a mathematical lower bound of Omega(N log N).

True-False.statement: No comparison-based sorting algorithm can achieve an average-case time complexity faster than O(N log N).
True-False.explanation: Any comparison sort corresponds to a decision tree with N! leaves, requiring height >= log2(N!) = Omega(N log N).

True-False.statement: Binary search on a sorted array of size N takes O(N) time in the worst case.
True-False.explanation: Binary search halves the search space each iteration, achieving O(log N) worst-case time complexity.

True-False.statement: QuickSort worst-case time complexity is O(N^2) when poor pivot selection causes maximally unbalanced partitions.
True-False.explanation: If the pivot is always the minimum or maximum element (e.g. sorted array with first element as pivot), QuickSort degrades to O(N^2).

True-False.statement: The worst-case time complexity of Quicksort is O(n^2), occurring when the chosen pivot is always the maximum or minimum element.
True-False.explanation: When pivots divide partitions into sizes 0 and n-1, recurrence becomes T(n) = T(n-1) + O(n), yielding O(n^2).

True-False.statement: Any comparison-based sorting algorithm requires at least Omega(n log n) comparisons in the worst case to sort n elements.
True-False.explanation: A decision tree of n! permutations requires height log2(n!) = Omega(n log n) to distinguish all possible orderings.

True-False.statement: Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm operates correctly on graphs with negative edge weights.
True-False.explanation: Dijkstra assumes distances are monotonically non-decreasing. Negative edge weights require the Bellman-Ford algorithm.

True-False.statement: Dynamic Programming requires two key properties: Optimal Substructure and Overlapping Subproblems.
True-False.explanation: Optimal substructure enables building global solutions from subproblems; overlapping subproblems allows memoization of repeated work.

True-False.statement: If a problem is in NP-Complete, it can definitely be solved in polynomial time O(n^k) on a deterministic Turing machine.
True-False.explanation: NP-Complete problems can be VERIFIED in polynomial time, but whether they can be SOLVED in polynomial time is the unsolved P vs NP question.

True-False.statement: Counting Sort can sort n integers in O(n + k) time where k is the maximum key value, without performing element-to-element comparisons.
True-False.explanation: Counting sort tallies occurrences into a frequency array, bypassing the Omega(n log n) comparison lower bound.

True-False.statement: Breadth-First Search (BFS) is guaranteed to find the path with the fewest edges between two vertices in an unweighted graph.
True-False.explanation: BFS explores vertices level by level, ensuring that the first time a destination is visited, it was reached via the minimal edge count.

Data Structures.introduction: Data Structures organize and store data to enable efficient access, modification, and traversal algorithms.
Data Structures.remediation: Contrast contiguous array memory (O(1) indexing, cache friendly) with node-based pointer structures (dynamic sizing, pointer overhead).
Data Structures.deep_dive: Arrays provide O(1) random access but O(N) insertion/deletion. Linked lists allow O(1) insertions at known nodes but require O(N) traversal and suffer poor cache locality. Hash tables provide O(1) average lookup via hash functions with collision resolution (separate chaining vs open addressing). Self-balancing binary search trees (AVL, Red-Black) guarantee O(log N) lookups, insertions, and deletions.

True-False.statement: Hash table lookups are guaranteed to be O(1) in the worst case regardless of hash collisions.
True-False.explanation: If all keys hash to the same bucket (worst-case collision), lookup degrades to O(N) unless balanced trees are used (which gives O(log N)).

True-False.statement: A Min-Heap guarantees that the root element is always the minimum element in the entire data structure.
True-False.explanation: By heap property, parent <= children everywhere, ensuring the root holds the global minimum in O(1) access time.

True-False.statement: In an AVL tree, the balance factor (height of left subtree minus height of right subtree) of any node is strictly limited to -1, 0, or +1.
True-False.explanation: If a balance factor reaches +/-2 after an insert or delete, tree rotations are performed to restore AVL balance.

True-False.statement: Accessing an arbitrary element by index in a singly linked list has O(1) time complexity.
True-False.explanation: Linked lists do not provide random access; accessing index k requires traversing k pointers from the head, which is O(n).

True-False.statement: A binary Min-Heap guarantees that for every node with a parent, parent.key <= node.key.
True-False.explanation: The min-heap property ensures that the root node always contains the minimum element in the entire heap.

True-False.statement: Bloom filters can return false positives (claiming an element is present when it isn't), but will NEVER return false negatives.
True-False.explanation: If all k hash bits for an element are 1, it might be a collision (false positive). If any bit is 0, the item was definitely never inserted.

True-False.statement: A Hash Table with Open Addressing stores colliding elements in linked lists allocated outside the primary bucket array.
True-False.explanation: Separate Chaining uses external linked lists. Open Addressing stores all entries within the primary array using probing.

True-False.statement: A Trie (Prefix Tree) lookup for a word of length m has time complexity O(m), independent of the total number of words stored.
True-False.explanation: Lookup follows m character edges in sequence, making performance depend only on key length.

True-False.statement: In a Red-Black tree, every path from the root to any descendant leaf must contain the exact same number of black nodes.
True-False.explanation: This Black-Height invariant ensures that the longest path is at most twice as long as the shortest path, guaranteeing O(log n) height.

Automata & Discrete Mathematics.introduction: Automata theory and Discrete Mathematics provide formal models of computation, state machines, logic, and discrete structures.
Automata & Discrete Mathematics.remediation: Focus on the Chomsky hierarchy (Regular, Context-Free, Turing-recognizable) and propositional logic equivalences.
Automata & Discrete Mathematics.deep_dive: Deterministic Finite Automata (DFA) recognize Regular Languages and lack memory beyond finite states. Pushdown Automata (PDA) add a single stack, recognizing Context-Free Languages. Turing Machines possess an infinite tape and define Turing-computability; the Halting Problem proves undecidability for general program termination.

True-False.statement: A Deterministic Finite Automaton (DFA) can recognize the language L = {a^n b^n | n >= 0}.
True-False.explanation: By the Pumping Lemma for Regular Languages, a DFA cannot count arbitrary numbers of symbols because it has finite memory. This language requires a Pushdown Automaton (PDA).

True-False.statement: The Halting Problem is undecidable: no general algorithm can determine whether an arbitrary program will eventually halt.
True-False.explanation: Proven by Alan Turing in 1936 using a diagonalization argument.

True-False.statement: Deterministic Finite Automata (DFA) and Non-deterministic Finite Automata (NFA) recognize the exact same class of languages (Regular Languages).
True-False.explanation: By the Powerset Construction (subset construction), every NFA can be converted to an equivalent DFA with at most 2^k states.

True-False.statement: The Halting Problem is undecidable: no general Turing machine can determine whether an arbitrary program will halt on a given input.
True-False.explanation: Alan Turing proved this fundamental theorem in 1936 using Cantor's diagonal argument.

True-False.statement: Standard regular expressions (without backreferences) can recognize the language of balanced parentheses { a^n b^n | n >= 0 }.
True-False.explanation: Regular expressions lack memory/stack to count arbitrary matching nesting. This requires a Context-Free Grammar / Pushdown Automaton.

True-False.statement: An undirected graph is bipartite if and only if it contains no odd-length cycles.
True-False.explanation: A graph can be 2-colored (bipartite) if and only if every cycle has an even number of vertices.

True-False.statement: Every connected acyclic graph (tree) with n vertices contains exactly n - 1 edges.
True-False.explanation: This is a fundamental theorem of graph theory provable by induction.

True-False.statement: In propositional logic, the conditional statement P -> Q is logically equivalent to (NOT P) OR Q.
True-False.explanation: Material implication is false only when P is True and Q is False; in all other cases (NOT P) OR Q evaluates to True.

True-False.statement: By De Morgan's Laws, NOT (A AND B) is logically equivalent to (NOT A) AND (NOT B).
True-False.explanation: De Morgan's law flips the operator: NOT (A AND B) is equivalent to (NOT A) OR (NOT B).

Allows programs to run without a CPU

Automatically parallelizes sequential for-loops onto GPU threads
Prevents stack overflow exceptions at compile time

True-False.statement: In database ACID transactions, Atomicity guarantees that either all statements in a transaction execute successfully, or all changes are rolled back.
True-False.explanation: Atomicity ensures an all-or-nothing guarantee, preventing partial updates during failures.

True-False.statement: In the CAP theorem, a distributed database under network partition can simultaneously provide both strong Consistency and 100% Availability.
True-False.explanation: Under network partition (P), a distributed system MUST choose between Consistency (C) or Availability (A).

True-False.statement: A B+ Tree stores all actual table record data pointers in the leaf nodes, while internal nodes only store routing search keys.
True-False.explanation: Keeping data only in leaf nodes maximizes the fanout of internal nodes, minimizing the number of disk I/O operations required per search.

True-False.statement: An SQL INNER JOIN returns rows only when there is at least one matching row in both joined tables.
True-False.explanation: If a row in Table A has no match in Table B according to the ON predicate, it is omitted from the result set.

True-False.statement: Redis stores all primary dataset keys in memory, making read and write latency typically sub-millisecond.
True-False.explanation: Redis is an in-memory key-value data structure store, using memory for primary reads/writes with optional asynchronous disk persistence.

True-False.statement: Database normalization to Third Normal Form (3NF) aims to eliminate transitive dependencies and minimize data redundancy.
True-False.explanation: 3NF requires the relation to be in 2NF and every non-prime attribute to be non-transitively dependent on the primary key.

True-False.statement: In database normalization, Third Normal Form (3NF) requires that every non-key column is non-transitively dependent on the primary key.
True-False.explanation: 3NF ensures each column depends on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key.

True-False.statement: NoSQL document stores like MongoDB strictly enforce compile-time schema validation across all foreign key relationships.
True-False.explanation: Document stores are schema-flexible, storing nested BSON/JSON documents without rigid relational foreign key constraints.

True-False.statement: Database indexes improve SELECT query performance but incur a write penalty during INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE operations.
True-False.explanation: Every mutation must also update index B-trees or hash maps on disk.

True-False.explanation: Alan Turing proved in 1936 that no general algorithm can determine if an arbitrary program halts on an arbitrary input.

True-False.statement: Moore's Law is a fundamental law of physics dictating quantum transistor tunneling limits.

True-False.statement: A Turing machine with a two-way infinite tape can compute strictly more functions than a standard one-way infinite tape Turing machine.

True-False.statement: Turing completeness means a computing system can simulate any single-taped Turing machine given sufficient time and memory.

True-False.statement: The Halting Problem proven by Alan Turing is decidable: an algorithm exists that can determine if any arbitrary program will halt.
True-False.explanation: Turing proved by diagonalization that no general algorithm can decide whether arbitrary programs will halt.

True-False.statement: Two's complement representation allows binary addition and subtraction to be executed by identical CPU ALU hardware.

Software Engineering.introduction: Software Engineering applies systematic, disciplined, and quantifiable engineering methodologies to the design, development, verification, and maintenance of complex software systems.
Software Engineering.remediation: Review design patterns, SOLID principles, testing pyramids, CI/CD deployment pipelines, and architectural patterns (microservices, event-driven, hexagonal).
Software Engineering.deep_dive: Software architecture demands balancing non-functional requirements including maintainability, fault tolerance, horizontal scalability, latency SLAs, and evolutionary architecture.

True-False.statement: The Single Responsibility Principle (SRP) states a class should have one, and only one, reason to change.
True-False.explanation: SRP (the S in SOLID) enforces high cohesion by giving each module responsibility over a single actor or concern.

True-False.statement: Integration tests are executed faster and with fewer external dependencies than unit tests.
True-False.explanation: Unit tests run fastest in isolation without external dependencies; integration tests verify communication across modules/databases and run slower.

True-False.statement: In Continuous Integration (CI), developers merge code into a shared mainline branch multiple times a day with automated builds and tests.
True-False.explanation: CI minimizes integration debt through frequent merges and automated regression verification.

True-False.statement: The Open-Closed Principle means software entities should be open for modification and closed for extension.
True-False.explanation: Open-Closed states software should be open for EXTENSION but closed for MODIFICATION.

True-False.statement: Dependency Injection decouples object creation from object usage, improving modularity and testability.
True-False.explanation: Injecting dependencies allows swapping real services with mocks/stubs during automated testing.

True-False.statement: The Single Responsibility Principle (SRP) states that a class or module should have one, and only one, reason to change.
True-False.explanation: SRP minimizes coupling and isolates the impact of requirement changes.

True-False.statement: In Test-Driven Development (TDD), production code is written first, and unit tests are written afterwards during QA staging.
True-False.explanation: TDD follows Red-Green-Refactor: write a failing test first, write minimal code to pass, then refactor.

True-False.statement: The Open/Closed Principle (OCP) states that software entities should be open for extension, but closed for modification.
True-False.explanation: New functionality should be added via inheritance, interfaces, or composition without editing existing tested source code.

True-False.statement: Event-driven architecture with CQRS decouples write operations (commands) from read operations (queries), allowing independent scaling.
True-False.explanation: CQRS enables optimized read models (e.g. Elasticsearch or Redis) distinct from transactional write schemas.

Cloud & Distributed Computing.introduction: Cloud & Distributed Computing studies networked computers coordinating actions via message passing to present a unified, high-availability computing system.
Cloud & Distributed Computing.remediation: Understand the CAP theorem, fallacies of distributed computing, consensus algorithms (Paxos, Raft), vector clocks, and horizontal vs vertical scaling.
Cloud & Distributed Computing.deep_dive: Distributed systems must manage partial failures, network partitions, split-brain conditions, eventual consistency models, and multi-region replication protocols.

True-False.statement: According to the CAP theorem, a distributed data store can simultaneously guarantee Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance.
True-False.explanation: In the presence of a network partition (P), a distributed system must choose between Consistency (C) and Availability (A).

True-False.statement: Horizontal scaling involves adding more memory or CPU cores to a single existing server instance.
True-False.explanation: Horizontal scaling (scale-out) adds more server nodes; vertical scaling (scale-up) adds resources to a single node.

True-False.statement: An idempotent operation can be applied multiple times without changing the result beyond the initial application.
True-False.explanation: Idempotency (e.g. HTTP PUT or DELETE) ensures network retries do not produce unintended duplicate side effects.

True-False.statement: In an eventually consistent database, all replicas will return the latest write immediately without any latency delay.
True-False.explanation: Eventual consistency allows replicas to return stale data temporarily until synchronization messages propagate across the network.

True-False.statement: According to the CAP theorem, a distributed data store can simultaneously provide Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance during a network partition.
True-False.explanation: When network partition (P) occurs, a distributed system MUST choose between Consistency (C) or Availability (A).

True-False.statement: In the Raft consensus algorithm, all log entries flow strictly in one direction: from the elected Leader to the Followers.
True-False.explanation: Raft simplifies consensus by ensuring followers only accept log entries appended by the current term's leader.

True-False.statement: Horizontal pod autoscaling in Kubernetes scales applications by increasing CPU and RAM allocations on existing nodes rather than creating new pod replicas.
True-False.explanation: Horizontal autoscaling creates new pod replicas; vertical autoscaling adjusts resource limits of existing containers.

Discrete Mathematics.remediation: Focus on set theory, propositional logic, graph theory, combinatorics, modular arithmetic, recurrence relations, and mathematical induction proofs.
Discrete Mathematics.deep_dive: Discrete math provides the formal proof techniques (pigeonhole principle, proof by contradiction) and structural models (posets, lattices, Markov chains) underpinning computing.

True-False.statement: The Pigeonhole Principle states that if N items are placed into K containers with N > K, at least one container must contain more than one item.
True-False.explanation: This fundamental counting principle is widely used in hash table collision proofs and compression limits.

True-False.statement: In propositional logic, p -> q (implication) is logically equivalent to (NOT p) OR q.
True-False.explanation: An implication is only false when p is true and q is false; otherwise it evaluates to true.

Asymptotic Complexity Analysis.introduction: Asymptotic complexity mathematically classifies algorithm resource utilization (time and memory) as input scale N approaches infinity.
Asymptotic Complexity Analysis.remediation: Big-O denotes asymptotic upper bound f(N) <= c*g(N); Big-Omega denotes lower bound; Big-Theta denotes tight bound.
Asymptotic Complexity Analysis.deep_dive: Amortized complexity uses aggregate analysis, accounting credits, or potential functions to prove guaranteed average time per operation across worst-case sequences.

True-False.statement: If an algorithm runs in O(N) time, it is also mathematically correct to say it runs in O(N^2) time.
True-False.explanation: Big-O represents an upper bound; anything bounded above by N is strictly bounded above by N^2.

True-False.statement: Big-Theta notation indicates a tight asymptotic bound where upper bound Big-O and lower bound Big-Omega coincide.
True-False.explanation: f(n) is Theta(g(n)) if and only if f(n) is O(g(n)) and f(n) is Omega(g(n)).

True-False.statement: An algorithm with time complexity O(2^N) executes faster for large N than an algorithm with O(N^3).
True-False.explanation: Exponential complexity O(2^N) explodes exponentially and is far slower than polynomial O(N^3) as N grows.

True-False.statement: Dijkstra's algorithm correctly computes shortest paths in graphs with negative weight edge cycles.

True-False.statement: Dynamic programming is applicable when a problem exhibits optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems.

Cybersecurity & Cryptography.introduction: Cybersecurity investigates threat modeling, public-key cryptography, authorization protocols, and defenses against memory and network exploits.
Cybersecurity & Cryptography.remediation: Focus on asymmetric vs symmetric key distribution, cryptographic salt uniqueness, and defense-in-depth principles (Zero Trust).

True-False.statement: Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS) ensures that compromise of a server's long-term private key cannot decrypt previously recorded network traffic.
True-False.explanation: PFS generates unique ephemeral session keys (ECDHE) for each TLS session so old traffic remains indecipherable.

True-False.statement: In a SQL injection attack, attackers exploit flaws where user inputs are concatenated directly into raw database command strings.
True-False.explanation: Parameterized queries and prepared statements completely neutralize SQL injection by separating code from data.

True-False.statement: Zero Trust network architecture assumes that any device inside the internal corporate network firewall can be inherently trusted.
True-False.explanation: Zero Trust operates under 'Never Trust, Always Verify', enforcing mutual TLS and per-request authorization internally.

True-False.statement: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) occurs when an application includes untrusted data in a web page without proper escaping, allowing malicious script execution.
True-False.explanation: XSS allows attackers to hijack session cookies, deface DOM elements, or redirect users to malicious endpoints.

True-False.statement: A cryptographic salt should be kept top-secret alongside the server's master root key in an encrypted vault.

True-False.statement: Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) achieves equivalent security to RSA with significantly smaller key sizes (e.g. 256-bit ECC ≈ 3072-bit RSA).

Sequencing.prompt: Order the lifecycle phases of an automated CI/CD deployment pipeline
ordered_sequence: Developer pushes code commit and opens pull request
CI server checks out code, runs linter, and builds executable artifacts
Unit, integration, and security static analysis (SAST) test suites execute
Container image is built, tagged with git commit SHA, and pushed to registry
CD engine deploys image to staging, runs smoke tests, and promotes to production

Sequencing.prompt: Order the incident response steps when a critical production alert fires
ordered_sequence: On-call engineer acknowledges alert and establishes incident communication channel
Initial triage determines severity, blast radius, and triggers rollback or mitigation
Service health is stabilized (traffic rerouted, canary halted, or caches flushed)
Detailed root cause investigation inspects logs, traces, and metrics
Blameless post-mortem document is drafted to identify systemic preventative action items
